@graph.headline: The BAA Is Not a Vault: What HIPAA and Attorney-Client Privilege Actually Require From Your AI
@graph.description: A signed business associate agreement allocates responsibility for protected health information. It does not keep that information inside your building — and for law firms, no such agreement exists at all. Here is what HIPAA and ABA Formal Opinion 512 actually require.

about.name: The distinction between a HIPAA business associate agreement and actual custody of protected health information — the required BAA elements under 45 CFR 164.504(e), the absence of any audit-right requirement in the HIPAA Rules, the proposed HIPAA Security Rule update and its July 2027 final-rule target, ABA Formal Opinion 512 and the Rule 1.6 informed-consent requirement for self-learning AI tools, and on-premises Local LLM architecture as the data path that removes third-party disclosure

keywords: can I use AI with PHI

mainEntity.name: Does a signed BAA make cloud AI HIPAA-compliant?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The agreement is required before protected health information is disclosed, but compliance also depends on the safeguards actually implemented, the subprocessors involved, and what you can document. A signature proves intent, not compliance.

mainEntity.name: Can we use AI on patient information if the vendor signs a BAA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if the vendor will bind every subcontractor, accept your training and retention terms, and give you evidence you can put in an audit file. Without those in writing, the agreement is thinner than it looks.

mainEntity.name: Do law firms need a BAA to use AI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not usually — firms are not covered entities, so HIPAA's business associate mechanics do not apply to client matters. The governing duty is Rule 1.6 confidentiality, and ABA Formal Opinion 512 requires informed client consent before inputting representation information into a self-learning tool.

mainEntity.name: Is a local LLM automatically HIPAA-compliant?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It removes the third-party disclosure problem, often the hardest one. You still owe encryption, access control, backups, training, incident response, and an annual risk analysis, and a vendor with remote access puts a third party back in the room.

mainEntity.name: What does the proposed HIPAA Security Rule change, and when?

acceptedAnswer.text: It would make encryption, multifactor authentication, segmentation, and anti-malware mandatory, add annual penetration tests and six-month vulnerability scans, and require an annual risk analysis built on an asset inventory and data-flow map. The final rule is slated for July 2027; timetables are not binding.

mainEntity.name: What is the cheapest defensible path for a small practice?

acceptedAnswer.text: De-identify what does not need identity, keep identifiable data out of tools you cannot audit, and put the rest on hardware you control. That sequence costs less than a breach and survives whichever Security Rule lands.
